blocks.heading: The elements must fit together
blocks.text: A business plan includes a description of the business, market research, a marketing plan, production plan, organisational plan, financial plan and action plan. The description establishes the proposal and objectives. Research supports demand assumptions; marketing explains the target and offering; production explains how output will be supplied; organisation allocates responsibilities; finance sets out needs, sources and forecasts; the action plan turns decisions into timed tasks. These are connected components, not interchangeable names. Compare assumptions across them: a large sales target is inconsistent with too little capacity unless the plan explains how capacity will change. A production schedule alone leaves ownership, demand and finance unanswered.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Bags predicts many orders but its production plan provides one worker and equipment capable of much less output. The sections need reconciliation before commitment. Either establish feasible extra resources or revise the sales expectation; copying the high forecast into every section does not make it realistic.

blocks.heading: Description of the business
blocks.text: This component identifies the proposed activity, ownership arrangement, location, objectives and main offering. It gives readers a clear basis for understanding the remaining sections. State a realistic purpose and scope rather than claiming the enterprise will be successful because it exists. The description is not a substitute for evidence of demand or a cash forecast.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Meals proposes a sole-owned weekday lunch collection service near a workplace cluster in Tsumeb. Original description: provide one affordable portable lunch range to nearby workers, begin with a limited trial and review repeat paid orders before expanding. The scope makes later capacity and marketing decisions more specific.

blocks.heading: Market research in the plan
blocks.text: The research component records the information supporting demand and customer assumptions, including sources, methods, findings and limitations. Show why the information fits the target market and what remains untested. Old regional data or favourable comments alone may not establish local paid demand. The plan should identify the next evidence needed, not hide uncertainty behind a precise-looking sales figure.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Hela Lunches has neutral interviews with nearby workers but no paid-sales trial. Its plan can report preferences and the sample limit, then schedule a small trial at the proposed price. It should not label every interested interviewee a confirmed daily customer.

blocks.heading: Marketing plan
blocks.text: The marketing plan states target customers, marketing objectives and coordinated choices of product, price, promotion and distribution. It explains how the enterprise will reach and serve its chosen market within a budget. It differs from research, which provides evidence, and from a single advertisement, which is one action. Targets should be reviewable and consistent with operational capacity.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Meals can prepare one weekday range and use local collection. Original marketing plan: target nearby workers seeking quick lunch; offer a portable meal at a tested feasible price; use a small accessible notice and direct information to nearby workplaces; provide prearranged collection; limit initial orders to confirmed capacity; review paid orders and repeat purchases weekly. This connects customer need with the whole offer.

blocks.heading: Production plan
blocks.text: The production plan explains how goods or services will be supplied: methods, equipment, inputs, suppliers, premises, capacity, timing and quality arrangements. It translates the sales proposal into a feasible operation. Job, batch and flow production are different methods developed in topic 4.5; the selected method must fit volume and variety. The plan is one part of the whole document, not the entire business plan.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Meals will prepare a limited set of lunches before collection. Its production component should specify ingredient supply, safe preparation resources, staff tasks, maximum feasible daily meals, collection timing and quality checks. Unconfirmed sales above that capacity need a revised operation, not an unexplained promise.

blocks.heading: Organisational plan
blocks.text: The organisational plan identifies roles, responsibilities, staffing and reporting. It shows who will carry out the proposed work and which skills are needed. A small business still needs responsibility for buying, production, customer contact and records even when one person performs several roles. Include relevant development needs; training may be on-the-job or off-the-job as explained in topic 3.5. A list of impressive titles does not provide the people or capabilities.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Eha Bags has one owner and one assistant. The plan can allocate purchasing and finance oversight to the owner and specified preparation work to the assistant, while stating who checks quality and handles customers. Tasks should fit available time rather than assume one person can do everything simultaneously.

blocks.heading: Financial plan
blocks.text: The financial plan identifies start-up and operating needs, finance sources, expected income and costs and cash timing. Explain assumptions and whether funding is agreed or only proposed. Profit forecasts and cash forecasts answer different questions: a credit sale can add profit before receipt. Test whether payments fall due before funds arrive. A lender assesses viability and repayment, so a document full of unsupported optimistic figures is weak evidence.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Ota Crafts expects to buy materials before collecting customer payments. The plan should show the material-payment dates and likely receipts, identify the temporary funding need and state how it would be covered. Calling the future sale profitable does not resolve that timing gap.

blocks.heading: Action plan
blocks.text: An action plan turns the proposal into specific tasks, responsible people, deadlines and dependencies. It lets managers coordinate implementation and check progress. A deadline should allow prerequisite work: equipment cannot be tested before it is obtained and staff cannot use a process safely before relevant preparation. Review missed tasks and revise the schedule where necessary rather than record dates without follow-up.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Meals plans a limited launch after checking demand and resources. Original action extract: owner completes customer-price trial in week 1; owner confirms input supplier and capacity in week 2; team tests preparation and collection in week 3; owner reviews finance before accepting week-4 orders. Each later task depends on the preceding evidence and resources.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why fictional Oru Bags’ equipment list and production schedule are not its entire business plan.

They belong to the production component, explaining how output can be made. The wider plan also needs the business description, research, marketing, organisation, finance and action arrangements. A technically feasible process alone does not establish customers or cash availability.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Business-plan components and usefulness
blocks.text:
Fictional Hela Meals has checked equipment capacity and preparation costs for a small service. Its draft plan includes marketing, production, organisation, finance and an action timetable, but sales rely on the owner’s guess rather than customer evidence. The owner has time for one further investigation before deciding whether to commit.

a(i) Define a business plan. [2]
a(ii) State two uses of a business plan. [2]
b State two operational details a business plan should explain. [2]
c Explain why Hela’s market and financial sections must be connected. [6]
d Evaluate whether investigating demand or repeating the equipment check should be the next priority. [8]

a(i) A document containing business objectives and important details of operations and finance. a(ii) Reviewing goals and communicating a finance proposal. b Required equipment and staffing responsibilities. c Sales assumptions determine expected income and production volume, which affect input spending and cash needs. Unsupported demand can therefore make an apparently precise financial forecast unreliable. Research findings should update both marketing and finance, not sit as an unrelated appendix. d Demand is the critical untested assumption, while capacity is already checked. Prioritise suitable customer and price evidence, recognising that research costs time and still cannot guarantee sales. Retain the equipment and other sections; prioritising one investigation does not justify omitting required components.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Business-plan components and usefulness
blocks.text:
Fictional Ota Bags has a coherent draft plan and verified workshop capacity and costs. Demand at its proposed price remains untested. The owner compares further market investigation with repeating the completed capacity check. For part (b) only, a dependable paid-order agreement now verifies sufficient demand at the proposed price, while the intended machine becomes unavailable and replacement capacity is unknown. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate demand research against another capacity check at Ota under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate the priority after the order agreement and machine change. Explain whether the judgement changes. [12]

a Demand is the missing evidence with consequences across the forecast, so prioritise suitable customer and price research. Repeating verified capacity work is less useful unless new facts question it. The plan should schedule the research and update all affected assumptions. b Demand now has dependable paid-order support, but unavailable machinery makes capacity uncertain. Prioritise the production alternative and its cost, timing and financing before promising delivery. The recommendation changes because the unresolved constraint changes. Update the action and financial plans too; do not discard marketing or assume the new machine will be affordable simply because orders exist.
